cards.scenario: External auditor from own AWS account needs read-only access across all accounts.
cards.ok: IAM role in each account with trust policy naming the auditor's ARN and read-only permissions.
cards.bad: Create an IAM user with access keys and read-only permissions for the auditor.
cards.why: Roles give temporary credentials revocable after the audit; IAM user access keys are long-term credentials, less secure.

cards.scenario: EC2 web app generates S3 pre-signed URLs for upload/download and checks object existence; access S3 securely.
cards.ok: IAM role allowing list and upload on the bucket, attached to the instance; app fetches temporary credentials from instance metadata.
cards.bad: Store access keys inside the EC2 instance and have the app read them.
cards.why: Roles supply temporary credentials via instance metadata; stored keys need distribution and rotation. Role also needs list and upload.

cards.scenario: Mobile app connects directly to S3 and DynamoDB and handles authentication; MOST cost-effective and scalable.
cards.ok: Web identity federation with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, IAM role for the provider, app uses temporary security credentials.
cards.bad: Web identity federation via Cognito, but app uses access and secret keys.
cards.why: Federation yields temporary credentials mapped to an IAM role; the app must not embed long-term access and secret keys.

cards.scenario: Set up AWS Organizations across existing accounts for central policy and full administrative control with the LEAST effort.
cards.ok: Invite member accounts from the management account; create OrganizationAccountAccessRole in each member trusting the management account.
cards.bad: Rely on cross-account access alone, assuming management account automatically has full admin control.
cards.why: Invited accounts do not give automatic admin control; the OrganizationAccountAccessRole must be created in the member account.

cards.scenario: Ensure tags are always added on resource creation across Organization accounts using centralized provisioning tools and IaC (select two).
cards.ok: AWS Service Catalog tagging provisioned resources + CloudFormation Resource Tags property applying tags on creation.
cards.bad: AWS Config adding corresponding tags to resources the moment they are created.
cards.why: Config evaluates and flags resources after creation and does not tag at creation; Service Catalog and CloudFormation apply tags proactively.

cards.scenario: Developers create and configure AWS resources (Windows EC2) and view Organizations info; least privilege.
cards.ok: Attach the PowerUserAccess AWS managed policy to the IAM users.
cards.bad: Create an IAM role with AdministratorAccess and assign it to the IAM users.
cards.why: AdministratorAccess grants all actions on all resources; PowerUserAccess excludes IAM and Organizations but allows read of org info, which is least privilege.

cards.scenario: Third-party vendor with own AWS account needs least-privilege API access to discover EC2; credentials unusable by other third parties.
cards.ok: IAM role with needed permissions only; trust policy with ExternalId condition matching the vendor's unique customer ID.
cards.bad: IAM user with required permissions and access keys given to the vendor.
cards.why: Roles give temporary credentials and ExternalId stops other parties assuming it (confused deputy); shared long-term keys are insecure.

cards.scenario: On-premises LDAP over IPSec VPN; employees use corporate accounts to access AWS resources.
cards.ok: Custom identity broker authenticates against LDAP, then calls STS to assume an IAM role and returns temporary credentials.
cards.bad: Integrate LDAP directly with IAM so employees log into IAM with LDAP credentials.
cards.why: IAM cannot integrate LDAP directly; LDAP is not SAML compatible, so an identity broker obtaining STS temporary credentials is required.

cards.scenario: SCP allows only cloudtrail and iam actions; IAM policy allows s3:*. Account cannot create S3 bucket; root cause.
cards.ok: SCP is the cause: it does not explicitly allow the S3 actions needed to create a bucket.
cards.bad: IAM policy is the cause because it denies users all S3-related actions.
cards.why: The IAM policy actually allows S3; SCPs set maximum permissions and a replaced FullAWSAccess means S3 is not allowed, blocking bucket creation.

cards.scenario: VPC web app needs private dedicated connection to on-premises servers (select two).
cards.ok: BGP/MD5-capable on-premises network device + Direct Connect link between VPC and internal network.
cards.bad: Transit VPC between the on-premises data center and the VPC.
cards.why: Direct Connect plus a BGP-capable device gives the dedicated private link; a Transit VPC is not the needed approach.

cards.scenario: Dual-tunnel VPN between CGW and VGW; find the single point of failure to fix for high availability.
cards.ok: Add a second Customer Gateway in a different data center with another dual-tunnel VPN connection.
cards.bad: Second Virtual Gateway in another AZ plus a second Customer Gateway and VPN.
cards.why: Only one VGW can attach to a VPC, so redundancy must come from a second customer gateway and VPN connection.

cards.scenario: DB patch downloads via single NAT instance time out; find root cause and fix.
cards.ok: NAT instance sends FIN on connection timeout and does not continue connection; use a NAT Gateway instead.
cards.bad: Database servers not in a Placement Group; use Spread or Cluster placement group.
cards.why: Failures stem from NAT instance timeout behavior on internet downloads; placement groups affect inter-instance traffic, not patch downloads.

cards.scenario: Inspect network payloads reaching the application to reverse-engineer sophisticated attacks.
cards.ok: Traffic Mirroring on the instances' ENI sending mirrored traffic to a monitoring appliance for storage and inspection.
cards.bad: VPC flow log to an S3 bucket for analysis.
cards.why: Traffic Mirroring copies actual packets for content inspection; flow logs only record Layer 4 metadata, not payloads.

cards.scenario: Employees-only access from corporate network or Internet; app server not exposed to Internet.
cards.ok: SSL VPN in the public subnet with client software on workstations; app servers in a private subnet.
cards.bad: IPsec VPN for employees with application servers in a public subnet.
cards.why: Servers stay unexposed in a private subnet and reached via VPN; a public subnet still exposes the instances.

cards.scenario: EC2 Auto Scaling in public subnet must reach Aurora MySQL in private subnet; least-privilege recommended rules (select two).
cards.ok: EC2 SG outbound to DB SG on 3306 + Aurora SG inbound from EC2 SG on 3306.
cards.bad: Update inbound NACL of the private subnet to allow the public subnet CIDR on 3306.
cards.why: Security group rules referencing SGs are least privilege and stateful; NACL CIDR rules are broader and not needed here.

cards.scenario: AI traffic-monitoring portal with strict RPO/RTO, highly available and fault-tolerant; MOST suitable architecture.
cards.ok: Auto Scaling EC2 across three AZs behind ALB, Aurora with Aurora Replicas, Route 53 Alias record to the ELB.
cards.bad: DynamoDB, EC2 Auto Scaling over four AZs behind ALB, Route 53 A record to the ELB.
cards.why: Alias record is the correct Route 53 record type for an ELB and Aurora replicas give strict RPO/RTO; a plain A record to the ELB is not valid.

cards.scenario: Multiple domains serve SSL on ALB without re-provisioning certificates per new domain (select two).
cards.ok: CloudFront with dedicated-IP custom SSL for alternate domains + ALB listener with multiple certificates using SNI.
cards.bad: One wildcard certificate to cover sub-domains and different domains.
cards.why: Per the key, ALB SNI with multiple bound certificates and CloudFront custom SSL fit; a wildcard cert only covers sub-domains of one domain.

cards.scenario: CloudFront with ALB origin; enable end-to-end HTTPS from browser to origin.
cards.ok: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS in CloudFront, with an ACM-issued certificate on both CloudFront and origin ALB.
cards.bad: CloudFront default certificate with redirect to HTTPS, ACM certificate only on origin.
cards.why: The default CloudFront certificate is not valid for the site's own domain name; use ACM certificate for custom domain on CloudFront and ALB.

cards.scenario: Cut page load from 7s to under 3s for global audience; MOST cost-effective (select two).
cards.ok: ElastiCache caching layer for sessions and frequent DB queries + CloudFront caching of re-usable content.
cards.bad: Second regional installation with Route 53 latency-based routing.
cards.why: Caching and CDN cut load times cheaply; duplicating a full regional stack is costly.

cards.scenario: Quickly handle unpredictable web traffic bursts for on-premises 2-tier gaming store before sale in weeks.
cards.ok: CloudFront distribution with custom on-premises origin, customized cache behavior and TTL to offload traffic.
cards.bad: Migrate with VM Import, ASG on imported AMI, RDS read replica and replicate Oracle database to RDS.
cards.why: Time is short; CloudFront offloads traffic with little change to existing infrastructure, while a full migration is slow and risky.

cards.scenario: Region power outage; short recovery downtime allowed across multi-region ASG apps.
cards.ok: DNS active-active failover using latency-based routing to ELBs with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes.
cards.bad: Enable DNSSEC and failover to standby with Evaluate Target Health set to No.
cards.why: Health-evaluated latency routing sends users only to healthy Regions; DNSSEC only prevents spoofing and No keeps routing to failing targets.

cards.scenario: Cost-effective, faster worldwide download of 5GB game package for millions of users.
cards.ok: S3 website-hosted bucket with CloudFront distribution as origin; Route 53 entry points to CloudFront.
cards.bad: Auto Scaling EC2 fleet with EBS volumes behind ALB, Route 53 pointing to ALB.
cards.why: CloudFront serves from nearby edge locations for faster, cheaper downloads; EC2 fleets cost more and give no global edge caching.

cards.scenario: Require HTTPS between viewers and CloudFront using the default cloudfront.net domain (select two).
cards.ok: Viewer Protocol Policy Redirect HTTP to HTTPS or HTTPS Only + CloudFront default SSL/TLS certificate with that cache behavior setting.
cards.bad: Use a self-signed certificate in the ELB.
cards.why: Viewer-to-CloudFront HTTPS needs only viewer protocol policy; ELB certificate concerns origin HTTPS, and self-signed certificates are not allowed there.

cards.scenario: CloudFront cache hit ratio dropping because query strings are inconsistent in order and case; increase cache hit ratio.
cards.ok: Lambda@Edge viewer request function normalizing query parameters (sorted, lower case) before cache lookup.
cards.bad: Enable a "case insensitive" option for query string processing on the distribution.
cards.why: No such CloudFront option exists; normalizing order and case at the viewer request makes identical requests share one cached object.

cards.scenario: Media uploads, 30-min processing, queue backlog during business hours; migrate to AWS, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: SQS standard queue + EC2 Auto Scaling group scaled on queue length, output to S3.
cards.bad: SQS queue + Lambda invoked per message, output to S3.
cards.why: Lambda max runtime is 15 minutes, so 30-minute media jobs cannot finish; EC2 ASG scaled on queue length handles them.

cards.scenario: Tightly coupled HPC cluster of 1000 EC2 nodes on EFS performs poorly; maximize performance (select three).
cards.ok: Cluster placement group in a single AZ + EFA network interfaces + FSx for Lustre instead of EFS.
cards.bad: Spread instances across multiple AZs with EBS RAID 0 instead of EFS.
cards.why: Tightly coupled HPC needs low latency in one AZ; multi-AZ spreading hurts network performance, and FSx for Lustre outperforms EFS.

cards.scenario: ALB with ASG across 3 AZs spikes above 90% at events; recover quickly if one AZ fails; MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: Raise ASG capacity and thresholds across AZs; Reserved for steady load, On-Demand plus Spot for peak, scale down after.
cards.bad: Deploy six Reserved and Spot instances in each of the 3 AZs.
cards.why: Fixed static capacity wastes money off-peak; Auto Scaling with Reserved baseline and On-Demand/Spot peak is cheaper and absorbs an AZ loss.

cards.scenario: Lambda deploy shifting 10% then rest after 5 minutes; trace event source and downstream calls.
cards.ok: Canary deployment configuration plus active tracing to integrate AWS X-Ray.
cards.bad: Linear deployment configuration with AWS Config tracing event source and downstream calls.
cards.why: Canary shifts traffic in two increments; X-Ray active tracing gives tracing, while AWS Config cannot trace invocations.

cards.scenario: Zero-downtime AMI rollout via UpdateStack replacing old EC2 instances from CloudFormation template.
cards.ok: UpdatePolicy attribute with AutoScalingRollingUpdate policy on the AutoScalingGroup resource.
cards.bad: DeletionPolicy attribute with MinSuccessfulInstancesPercent on the LaunchConfiguration resource.
cards.why: UpdatePolicy rolling update replaces instances in batches automatically; DeletionPolicy only governs resource retention on stack deletion.

cards.scenario: Lambda/DynamoDB/OpenSearch ERP API: no downtime on failed deploy, prevent subsequent deployments, full capacity during deployment, MOST efficient.
cards.ok: CodeDeploy blue/green + CloudFormation for DynamoDB, Lambda, OpenSearch; Elastic Beanstalk with Immutable deployment policy.
cards.bad: Blue/green via CodeDeploy with SAM, Elastic Beanstalk set to All at Once.
cards.why: All at Once updates every instance together and risks downtime; Immutable launches a new full set, keeping full capacity and leaving originals untouched on failure.

cards.scenario: CI/CD deploying new versions several times an hour with quick rollback to previous version.
cards.ok: Elastic Beanstalk staging environment; deploy new version there, then swap staging and production URLs.
cards.bad: Bake AMI, update Auto Scaling launch template, scale out and terminate old instances.
cards.why: URL swap shifts traffic instantly and rolls back by swapping again; AMI rebuild and instance replacement is slow for hourly releases.

cards.scenario: CloudFormation template update caused major downtime; reduce downtime chances during deployments.
cards.ok: CodeBuild test stage on non-production + CloudFormation change sets to preview + CodeDeploy blue/green with quick rollback.
cards.bad: CodeDeploy blue/green then manually log in to instances to verify the deployment.
cards.why: Automated tests and change sets catch destructive changes before production; manual login verification is slow and error prone.

cards.scenario: Move multi-tier app with remote users facing latency; MOST cost-effective, MINIMAL change, improve uptime and user experience.
cards.ok: AppStream (WorkSpaces applications) for desktop apps, MySQL to Aurora, app/presentation tiers in Auto Scaling EC2 behind ALB.
cards.bad: WorkSpaces per user, self-hosted MySQL on a large EC2 instance, ECS containers behind ALB.
cards.why: Self-hosted MySQL on one EC2 hurts uptime and per-user WorkSpaces costs more; Aurora is managed and AppStream streams the desktop apps.

cards.scenario: Automate extraction of data from scanned forms, reduce human effort, keep high accuracy.
cards.ok: Step Functions + Lambda orchestrating Amazon Textract (OCR) and Comprehend, output to S3.
cards.bad: Rekognition and Transcribe with Step Functions, output in Amazon DocumentDB.
cards.why: Textract extracts text, forms and tables from scanned documents; Rekognition and Transcribe are for images and audio, not form data.

cards.scenario: RDS MySQL spikes during daily batch analytics and CRM becomes unresponsive; notify on-premises dashboard via SMTP email, automate.
cards.ok: RDS read replicas for batch analytics + SNS to notify the on-premises system by email.
cards.bad: RDS read replicas + Amazon SQS to notify the on-premises system.
cards.why: SQS cannot push email to an SMTP endpoint; SNS can send email notifications, and read replicas offload the batch reads.

cards.scenario: One-time EMR cluster, 20 TB, 30 instances, 48 hours; MOST cost-effective without sacrificing data integrity.
cards.ok: On-Demand master and core nodes, Spot instances for task nodes.
cards.bad: Reserved instances for master and core nodes, Spot for task nodes.
cards.why: Reserved instances need a 1-3 year commitment, wasteful for a one-time 48-hour run; On-Demand keeps core nodes stable and Spot handles tasks.

cards.scenario: Sudden unpredictable write spike during sale; ensure all submissions committed to DB without changing data model.
cards.ok: SQS queue between application and database, Lambda consuming messages and writing to the database.
cards.bad: Migrate the database to DynamoDB with automatic scaling.
cards.why: Moving to DynamoDB changes the data model, which is not allowed; SQS buffers writes durably and Lambda writes at a sustainable pace.

cards.scenario: Image analysis taking 20 hours per day on one EC2 instance and EBS volume; cut processing time, improve availability.
cards.ok: Store I/O files in S3, SQS to distribute work, Auto Scaling group scaled on SQS queue length.
cards.bad: EBS Provisioned IOPS volume, SNS for parallel hosts, scale on SNS notification count.
cards.why: EBS is just storage and SNS only notifies; S3 plus SQS with queue-length scaling enables parallel, available processing.

cards.scenario: App on EC2 with BASE-model on-premises DB over Direct Connect; erratic during heavy writes; cost-effective fix.
cards.ok: SQS queue for writes with a consumer process flushing the queue to the on-premises database.
cards.bad: Write to DynamoDB, feed table to an EMR cluster map function updating the on-premises database.
cards.why: EMR plus DynamoDB adds cost and complexity; SQS cheaply buffers writes, which suits an eventually consistent database.

cards.scenario: Improve reliability of overloaded EC2 MQTT broker losing sensor data to DynamoDB; cost-effective.
cards.ok: AWS IoT Core Data-ATS endpoint via Route 53 + IoT rule inserting directly into DynamoDB.
cards.bad: ASG of EC2 MQTT brokers behind NLB (Alias record) with EFS shared storage.
cards.why: IoT Core is managed, scales to many devices, and rules write straight to DynamoDB; self-managed brokers keep operational burden and EFS does not fix broker load.

cards.scenario: Prevent data loss when DynamoDB writes throttle; MOST cost-effective way to reduce table load.
cards.ok: SQS queue decoupling application from database, buffering writes until throttling subsides.
cards.bad: Replicate the table to another Region using global tables.
cards.why: SQS smooths traffic and holds items until the loader writes them; global tables are for multi-region fault tolerance and do not reduce load.

cards.scenario: Reduce page latency for Spot-EC2 portal with on-premises database; quick, cost-effective change.
cards.ok: ElastiCache for Redis in the VPC to cache queries, with Redis replication for read scaling and availability.
cards.bad: Migrate on-premises DB to Aurora with DMS/SCT and Aurora Replicas.
cards.why: Cache cuts DB round-trips to the data center quickly and cheaply; Aurora migration is slower and more costly.

cards.scenario: Near-real-time genomic data ingestion, parallel durable storage, analytics, output to data warehouse.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Streams collecting data, Kinesis client (KCL) analysis, then EMR saving results to Redshift.
cards.bad: Store inbound files in S3, use Kinesis with SQS for analysis, send results to Redshift.
cards.why: Kinesis Data Streams gives near-real-time, durable, parallel stream processing; S3 landing with SQS is not a real-time analytics path.

cards.scenario: Semi-structured data web service, handles load spikes, highly available and fault-tolerant across a regional failure.
cards.ok: DynamoDB global table in two Regions, on-demand capacity, Fargate behind ALB per Region, Route 53 latency routing with health checks.
cards.bad: Primary S3 bucket with Cross-Region Replication, API Gateway/Lambda per Region behind two CloudFront distributions with failover routing.
cards.why: DynamoDB global tables are multi-active, on-demand absorbs spikes, and Route 53 health checks fail over; S3 is not suited to read/write semi-structured data.

cards.scenario: Store 50 TB of written materials in AWS with searchable collection on dynamic website.
cards.ok: CloudFormation deploying S3 bucket storage, OpenSearch for search, and EC2 to host the website.
cards.bad: CodeDeploy deploying two S3 buckets, using native S3 search for search.
cards.why: S3 is great storage but lacks an effective search feature; OpenSearch provides full-text search over the collection.

cards.scenario: Detect new DynamoDB entries and automatically run Lambda tests on results, with minimal configuration changes.
cards.ok: Enable a DynamoDB stream and trigger the Lambda function from it.
cards.bad: Migrate the table to DocumentDB and use its EventBridge integration to invoke Lambda.
cards.why: DynamoDB Streams integrate natively with Lambda triggers on item changes; a database migration is far more change than needed.

cards.scenario: Migrate NGINX web server and Oracle RAC One Node database to AWS with automated backup.
cards.ok: EC2 for NGINX and database, EBS volumes, Data Lifecycle Manager scheduled snapshots.
cards.bad: RDS instance with automated backups on an RDS RAC cluster.
cards.why: RDS does not support Oracle RAC, so database must run on EC2; DLM automates snapshots and retention without scripts.

cards.scenario: Durable, cost-effective archive of sensitive data from on-premises tape backup infrastructure.
cards.ok: Tape Gateway backing up to S3, archiving to Glacier, using existing tape processes.
cards.bad: Stored Volume Gateway with point-in-time EBS snapshots.
cards.why: Volume Gateway is not for tape archives; Tape Gateway VTL keeps existing tape tooling and archives to Glacier cheaply.

cards.scenario: Collect configuration, usage, behavior data from on-premises servers for TCO analysis before migration.
cards.ok: AWS Application Discovery Service to gather on-premises data and support TCO analysis.
cards.bad: AWS Migration Hub to collect data from each server and do TCO.
cards.why: Migration Hub only tracks migration progress; Discovery Service collects configuration, usage and behavior data, exportable for TCO.

cards.scenario: Migrate 40 TB tape video files from MAM to AWS; auto-build object/face metadata catalog using existing people photos.
cards.ok: File Gateway to S3, Rekognition collection from people catalog, Lambda pulls metadata into MAM catalog.
cards.bad: DataSync to S3, SageMaker Jupyter notebook to build the collection, Lambda invokes SageMaker.
cards.why: Rekognition natively detects objects and faces and builds face collections; SageMaker needs custom model work and the MAM integration is awkward.

cards.scenario: Cross-Region DR for web service with MySQL on EC2; RPO under a minute, RTO under 5 minutes, low operational overhead.
cards.ok: Migrate to Aurora global database, us-east-1 primary and us-west-2 secondary, Route 53 failover with health checks.
cards.bad: Migrate to RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ, Route 53 failover to us-west-2.
cards.why: Multi-AZ stays in one Region; Aurora Global Database gives RPO about 1 second and RTO under 1 minute across Regions.

cards.scenario: Aurora 40 TB, stateless EC2 tiers, RTO 30 minutes, RPO 5 minutes, cost-effective DR (select two).
cards.ok: Daily copied EC2 snapshots to backup Region + Aurora cross-Region read replica promoted on disaster.
cards.bad: Hot-standby of web and application tiers in backup Region.
cards.why: Hot standby is costly and unnecessary for a 30-minute RTO; snapshot restore of stateless tiers is cheaper and replica meets the RPO.

cards.scenario: Windows CMS on 3+ multi-AZ instances needing identical data, Windows ACLs, AD join, LEAST management overhead.
cards.ok: New Windows AMI ASG across three AZs, FSx for Windows File Server shared storage, user data installs app, mounts share and joins AD.
cards.bad: EBS volume with Multi-Attach shared across instances in the ASG.
cards.why: FSx for Windows is fully managed SMB storage with native ACLs and AD integration; EBS Multi-Attach lacks a shared Windows file system and ACLs.

cards.scenario: 200 TB monthly 72-hour job needing high-performance shared access; largest overall storage cost reduction.
cards.ok: Data in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, lazy-loaded FSx for Lustre used only for the job then deleted.
cards.bad: EFS Standard-IA as shared filesystem mounted for the job.
cards.why: S3 plus a temporary FSx for Lustre gives cheap storage and high performance only when needed; EFS-IA stays costlier and slower.

cards.scenario: Gateway-stored volume (iSCSI) on-premises; DR requires running web app on AWS if on-premises fails. MOST suitable restore.
cards.ok: Generate EBS snapshot from the Storage Gateway volume, restore to an EBS volume, attach to the EC2 app server.
cards.bad: Attach the Storage Gateway directly to the EC2 instance hosting the app server.
cards.why: Stored volumes back up to S3 as EBS snapshots; you cannot attach a gateway directly, so snapshot then EBS volume is the restore path.

cards.scenario: KMS-encrypted Redshift cluster DR with recovery site at least 500 miles away; make architecture highly available.
cards.ok: Create a snapshot copy grant for a KMS key in the destination region and enable cross-region snapshot copy.
cards.bad: Enable cross-region snapshot copy without a snapshot copy grant.
cards.why: KMS keys are region specific, so an encrypted cluster needs a snapshot copy grant in the destination region for Redshift to encrypt there.

cards.scenario: WorkSpaces logins fail because 10 TB FSx for Windows profile file system is full; fix and prevent recurrence.
cards.ok: CloudWatch alarm on FreeStorageCapacity, EventBridge invokes Lambda that increases capacity with update-file-system.
cards.bad: New larger FSx file system, script to copy profiles, CloudWatch metric and SNS notification.
cards.why: FSx storage capacity can be increased in place via update-file-system and automated; building a new file system and copying data is manual and disruptive.

cards.scenario: Portal on EC2 can no longer upload via pre-signed URLs though developer laptop worked; valid reasons (select two).
cards.ok: Pre-signed URL expiry set too short + misconfigured AWS credentials on the portal's EC2 instances.
cards.bad: Enabling S3 versioning invalidates all pre-signed URLs.
cards.why: Versioning does not invalidate pre-signed URLs; tight expiry and missing or bad credentials on the EC2 instances explain the failure.

cards.scenario: Only authorized IAM users/roles may call API Gateway; inspect each request end-to-end for latency and service maps.
cards.ok: AWS_IAM authorization, execute-api:Invoke permission, SigV4 signing, and AWS X-Ray tracing.
cards.bad: CORS allowed-origin headers, execute-api:Invoke, and CloudWatch Logs for tracing.
cards.why: CORS does not authenticate callers and CloudWatch Logs gives no end-to-end service map; AWS_IAM plus X-Ray does.

cards.scenario: SSE-C for S3 bucket, data secure at rest and in transit (select two).
cards.ok: REST API requests with the three SSE-C customer-key headers + presigned URLs using the customer-algorithm header.
cards.bad: Use WSS (WebSocket Secure).
cards.why: SSE-C works through S3 request headers over HTTPS; WSS is not an S3 mechanism.

cards.scenario: Fully managed, encrypted at rest and in transit, durable, own rotated key, Redshift Spectrum analysis.
cards.ok: S3 bucket with SSE-KMS and bucket policy enforcing HTTPS-only connections.
cards.bad: Storage Gateway File Gateway with data stored in S3 using SSE-S3.
cards.why: SSE-S3 keys are S3-managed, so company cannot use its own rotated key; SSE-KMS with HTTPS-only policy meets all requirements.

cards.scenario: Confidential S3 files must not traverse the Internet; only the web portal's EC2 instances may access the bucket.
cards.ok: VPC endpoint policy for the bucket + IAM role on EC2 + bucket policy allowing only the VPC endpoint and that role.
cards.bad: Endpoint policy + bucket policy allowing only the VPC endpoint + NACL denying other instances to the S3 prefix list.
cards.why: Endpoint condition lets every instance in the VPC in, and NACLs are subnet-level. Identity needs an IAM role named in the bucket policy.

cards.scenario: Reduce DDoS attack surface and blast radius (select two).
cards.ok: Restrictive security group, origin behind CloudFront, Shield Advanced + NACLs allowing only required ports and AWS WAF blocking DDoS patterns.
cards.bad: Add ELB and Auto Scaling with extra-large instances, Session Manager filtering client web sessions.
cards.why: Session Manager is for admin shell access, not web traffic filtering; reducing exposed surface with Shield, WAF, CloudFront limits DDoS impact.

cards.scenario: Use company HSMs to generate key material for S3 log encryption at rest.
cards.ok: KMS key with EXTERNAL origin, import on-premises HSM key material via import token; bucket policy requires KMS, denies unencrypted.
cards.bad: New CloudHSM cluster as KMS key material source with 1-year rotation.
cards.why: Requirement is to use the company's existing HSMs; imported external key material does that, whereas CloudHSM cluster makes AWS-hosted HSM keys.

cards.scenario: Most durable and secure logging to track changes to all resources across all accounts globally.
cards.ok: Organization trail for all accounts and Regions, new S3 bucket, MFA Delete and log encryption.
cards.bad: One trail applied to all regions using an existing S3 bucket with MFA Delete only.
cards.why: Organization trail covers every member account centrally; the single-account all-regions trail misses other accounts and lacks encryption.

cards.scenario: Allow only private files in S3 bucket, no public read or write; MINIMAL effort.
cards.ok: Enable Amazon S3 Block Public Access on the bucket.
cards.bad: SCP via Organizations denying public objects, attached to the account.
cards.why: Block Public Access overrides policies and ACLs with one setting; an SCP cannot target object ACLs and adds effort.

cards.scenario: Protect multi-tier app from DDoS, SQL injection, HTTP floods and bad bots; MOST suitable, scalable.
cards.ok: AWS WAF and AWS Shield Advanced on all web endpoints, with WAF rules against SQL injection and common exploits.
cards.bad: NACL deny for suspect source IP with AWS Config auditing the rules.
cards.why: WAF plus Shield Advanced covers DDoS, SQLi, floods and bots at scale; blocking one IP does not stop distributed attacks.

cards.scenario: Automated CVE scan and tagging of new custom AMIs, plus 30-day rescans and patching (select two).
cards.ok: Lambda approval rules + SSM Parameter Store approved-AMI list + 30-day EventBridge cron triggering SSM Automation, plus Inspector assessment template CVE scans.
cards.bad: Lambda approval rules, Parameter Store AMI list, AWS Config managed rule scanning instances and running SSM Automation on findings.
cards.why: Config managed rules evaluate configuration compliance, not CVE scanning; Inspector scans CVEs and scheduled SSM Automation handles patching.

cards.scenario: Ensure running EC2 uses pre-approved AMIs without stalling agile CI/CD; check only after deployment; LEAST impact (select two).
cards.ok: AWS Config rule detecting non-approved AMIs + Lambda terminate and SNS notify; scheduled Lambda scanning running instances for unauthorized AMIs.
cards.bad: IAM policies restricting users to launch only from tagged pre-approved AMIs.
cards.why: IAM policies are preventive and block launches, stalling the pipeline; the requirement is to analyze after the release is deployed.

cards.scenario: Automatically find S3 objects containing PII at large volume and determine whether the data was accessed.
cards.ok: Enable Amazon Macie to classify and detect PII objects; track GET API calls in AWS CloudTrail.
cards.bad: Detect PII using Athena and track GET calls with CloudWatch.
cards.why: Athena cannot detect PII; Macie does ML-based discovery, and CloudTrail (not CloudWatch) records the GET API calls.

cards.scenario: Control Tower multi-account environment: centralize compliance and security findings with preventive, detective, responsive controls.
cards.ok: Create a member account, enable AWS Security Hub there and designate it the delegated administrator.
cards.bad: Enable GuardDuty in each account and export findings to a central S3 bucket for analysis.
cards.why: Security Hub aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Config, Inspector, Macie with a delegated admin; per-account GuardDuty export lacks central compliance view.

cards.scenario: One-time EMR cluster, 200 instances, ~8 hours; most cost-effective node purchasing.
cards.ok: On-Demand for master and core nodes, Spot for task nodes.
cards.bad: Reserved instances for master and core nodes, Spot for task nodes.
cards.why: Reserved needs long-term commitment, unsuitable for a one-off 8-hour job; On-Demand core nodes are safe for HDFS data while task nodes can be Spot.

cards.scenario: Org with consolidated billing: enforce cost center and project ID tags on existing and future RDS and DynamoDB resources.
cards.ok: Tag existing resources with Tag Editor, activate cost allocation tags in Billing, apply SCP on the OU denying creation without the tags.
cards.bad: Config rule emailing finance plus hourly cross-account Lambda that tags RDS and DynamoDB resources.
cards.why: SCP preventively enforces tags on future resources and Tag Editor covers existing ones; the Lambda approach is reactive and operationally heavy.

cards.scenario: Windows Server on EC2 must always have latest OS patches, patched even outside the maintenance window; LEAST administrative overhead.
cards.ok: Windows Server on EC2 with Systems Manager Patch Manager auto-approving patches via baselines.
cards.bad: Hardened Marketplace image hosted on AWS CloudShell, Patch Manager, and AppStream/WorkSpaces applications as bastion.
cards.why: CloudShell cannot host the server and AppStream bastion adds components; Patch Manager on EC2 alone automates patching with least effort.

cards.scenario: Patch known OS vulnerability on EC2 fleet quickly and record all patch and association compliance changes.
cards.ok: Systems Manager Patch Manager to deploy patches + AWS Config to record and evaluate compliance.
cards.bad: Build a new AMI that installs weekly OS patches and roll it out to the fleet.
cards.why: AMI approach gives no per-patch control and cumbersome rollback; Patch Manager deploys patches and Config records compliance changes.
